title: Goodbye Notch, Hello Invisible Face ID: Metalenz's Under-Display Breakthrough
summary:
You know that pill-shaped cutout at the top of your iPhone screen—the one Apple calls the Dynamic Island? It's there because the TrueDepth camera system needs a window to map your face. But what if that island could vanish, leaving you with a perfectly smooth, uninterrupted display? Boston-based optics startup Metalenz just demoed a way to make that happen, and it could change how we unlock our phones forever. 

At Display Week 2026 in Los Angeles, Metalenz showed its Polar ID facial authentication system working from beneath an OLED screen. Unlike traditional cameras that stack multiple glass or plastic lenses to focus light, Metalenz uses a single flat lens covered in nanostructures—a metasurface—that bends light with incredible precision. This slashes the space needed for the hardware. The company says over 300 million of its metasurfaces are already in consumer devices, mostly in time-of-flight sensors that capture depth for autofocus. 

But the real secret sauce is polarization. When light hits a material, it scatters in a pattern unique to that material's properties. Human skin has a polarization signature that's distinct from silicone, so even a high-quality 3D mask can't fool it. "We've now proven with multiple third parties that have done testing that we meet the highest security standards they have in terms of performance, in terms of keeping out masks and any mask of any quality," CEO Rob Devlin told WIRED. That's a big deal for Android phones, which have largely lacked a secure face unlock equivalent to Apple's Face ID—Google's Pixel face unlock can be spoofed with a convincing mask. 

Hiding the sensor under the display does cause some signal distortion and intensity loss, but Devlin says the polarization information remains largely intact. The demo showed the system easily recognizing his face and rejecting a 3D mask, even through the screen. To make it work, the display needs a slightly thinned-out region for the sensor, but Devlin says you can't even tell it's there. The company is in early talks with major smartphone manufacturers. 

Polar ID will first appear in consumer devices—phones and laptops—in 2027, with the under-display version likely following in 2028. For years, phone makers have chased the dream of a truly bezel-less, notch-free design. Some tried pop-up cameras; Samsung experimented with under-display selfie cams but suffered from poor image quality. Metalenz's approach sidesteps that problem because it doesn't need a high-resolution color image—just the polarization data. "Folks have decided to differentiate along a continuous display versus Apple's interrupted display," Devlin said. "So I think this is also something that can really offer face unlock in a truly seamless manner—seamless in the sense that you don't even feel like you're securely unlocking your phone when you are." 

If this tech takes off, your next phone might have a screen that's all screen, with no visible camera holes—just a glance and you're in, like magic.
why_it_matters: This technology could redefine smartphone design and security, influencing how all devices handle authentication and challenging the dominance of Apple's Face ID. For a generation that values both privacy and aesthetics, it means your next phone might be both more secure and more beautiful without compromise.

background_read: Apple's Face ID, introduced with the iPhone X in 2017, mapped faces with 30,000 infrared dots, setting a high bar for secure phone unlocking.
Android phones have struggled to match that security—many early face unlock systems could be fooled by a photograph or 3D mask.
Under-display cameras have been a holy grail for phone makers, with Samsung's first attempts resulting in soft, hazy selfies because the screen blocks too much light.
Metalenz, a Boston-based startup founded by Harvard physicists, has already shipped over 300 million of its flat lenses in time-of-flight sensors that help cameras focus quickly.
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA) originally funded metasurface research because of its potential for ultra-compact military optics.

perspectives.description: A truly seamless display removes distractions and feels more immersive. Combined with secure face unlock, it could make unlocking your phone feel almost like magic—fast, invisible, and reliable, finally delivering the full-screen promise that manufacturers have sought for years.

Under-display sensors could introduce new privacy risks if they are harder to physically cover or disable. Additionally, if the system relies heavily on polarization, any skin condition, extreme lighting, or occlusions might degrade performance, potentially locking users out in edge cases.

This represents a convergence of multiple fields—nanophotonics, machine learning, and display engineering—that has been decades in the making. The metasurface lens is part of a broader trend of shrinking optics without sacrificing quality, echoing the miniaturization that changed cameras decades ago.

If successful, under-display sensors could expand beyond face unlock to full health-monitoring sensors hidden in screens, making phones personal diagnostic tools. The technology might also appear in cars (driver monitoring), smart homes, and even augmented reality glasses, making interactions smoother and less obtrusive.
